The request: The owner wants the sessions worth reading found without reading them all, and wants their failures turned into benchmark cases. The morning when an anomaly-detection draft was built as a model of customer ids should be found by rule, by more than one detector.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
The owner wants the sessions worth reading found without reading them all, and wants their failures turned into benchmark cases. The morning when an anomaly-detection draft was built as a model of customer ids should be found by rule, by more than one detector.

(2) Plan
1. Detectors as pure rules over the shared event contract, so the main product can run the same ones on its own rows.
2. One read per visit, shared by the card and its flags.
3. Feedback as an event of kind feedback.given; on a yes or no decision, also a user_decision_exposed label saying the opposite.

(3) Decisions
- The data analysis's role for a column wins over its name. Because: country_code analysed as categorical is a category. A name is only a guess, so a hit on the name alone is medium severity, not high.
- Only blocking questions count for built_with_question_open, tracked per conversation. Because: Home lets a build go past the unit and action questions on purpose (dclab_core.card, blocks=False). An answer given in another conversation does not answer this one.
- A question asked again with different options is a follow-up, not a repeat. Because: Home asks for the outcome in words first, then asks again with the column options once the data arrives. That is the main flow, not a failure.
- Only someone who may change the work or review it turns "wrong" into a label, and only once. Because: A label weighs on what the decision models learn. A viewer's opinion is kept as feedback; duplicates would inflate the counts.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The card reads at most 5000 events a visit and the timeline 20000, so a very long visit's flags can differ between the two.
- The detectors are rules: their precision on real sessions is not yet measured (19.12 turns flagged sessions into benchmark cases).

(5) How you will know it is done
- planted faults: each fix undone fails a test
- the owner's morning: flagged by at least two detectors

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for

- A detector is chosen on anomalies planted in a validation period, never on the rows to review. Because: With no label, planted shapes are the only truth, and the rows to review play the holdout's part.

- A solution may have no target only for a kind that says it needs none. Because: Every other kind learns from an outcome, and a missing one must still be refused.
- Confirmed alerts become partial labels, their selection by the detector written in their provenance. Because: A rare-event model trained on them partly measures the detector again; the person must see that.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- No page shows the review list yet.
- Planted shapes are generic.

- the owner's morning with no label, four seeds: a review list at least ten times above the fake trips' rate, the rows to review read once, the limits stated

The request: Phase 1's last storage gap: the sets were rows of JSONL with no turn-level view, no model-call view, no columnar form, a manifest that did not say which redaction or which code produced it, and no rebuild after a deletion: a deleted project could stay in a set until someone ran make datasets. Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Phase 1's last storage gap: the sets were rows of JSONL with no turn-level view, no model-call view, no columnar form, a manifest that did not say which redaction or which code produced it, and no rebuild after a deletion: a deleted project could stay in a set until someone ran make datasets. Adoptable by the main product.

(2) Plan
1. The two builders as pure functions in the core, over exported events and the ledger's records: a turn from a person's message to the next, joined by ids and the time window.
2. Every number of an episode a count or a sum of events named in the row; without text=True, no free text at all.
3. A model call joined to its check by the request id and to the feedback on the message the request produced; the check becomes an event.
4. The columnar writer as an optional extra; the manifest names the redaction version, the code's commit and the files.
5. The rebuild: a marker left by a deletion, a day's age, one lock for every worker.

(3) Decisions
- A turn is the window from one person's message to the next, and the project's events of that window join it by the project id. Because: Stage runs and moves carry the project, not the draft or session a person talked in; the window is what ties a message to what it set going.
- Under improve alone an episode carries no decision and no text; the model calls are train only. Because: Decisions leave for train only, and a prompt or a reply is the model's text, the most it can be.
- A deletion leaves a marker and the next sweep rebuilds, rather than rebuilding inside the deletion. Because: A deletion must not wait on a build, and the worker already holds the lock and the services.
- Nested values become JSON text in the columnar file. Because: One type per column; the few nested columns read back with json.loads and the JSONL stays the source of truth.
- The check is joined by the request id of the context, and a Home reply joins its request only when it says a model wrote it. Because: A rule's reply after a model call must not inherit the call's check or feedback.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The check joins its call by the last model request of the context: a verdict right after another call could inherit it.
- A prompt the gateway kept is redacted by rule: a name written in lower case passes.

What the package must deliver:
dclab_core.tracing (parse and format the W3C traceparent, derive a trace id from a request id); Ids gains trace, span, parent_span (event v8); the edge continues or derives a trace and answers with a traceparent; events and log lines carry the ids; a job runs in the request's trace in its own span; a model request, an agent step and a tool call are spans; the record is read by trace (an indexed column on PostgreSQL).

The request: Phase 1's last observability gap: a request had an id, but a collector (OpenTelemetry, a log store) joins by trace and span ids; the log lines, the events, the jobs a request queued and its model requests shared no id that a tool could follow end to end. Adoptable by the main product.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Phase 1's last observability gap: a request had an id, but a collector (OpenTelemetry, a log store) joins by trace and span ids; the log lines, the events, the jobs a request queued and its model requests shared no id that a tool could follow end to end. Adoptable by the main product.

(2) Plan
1. The header and the derivation as pure functions in the core.
2. A trace context in observe that every event and log line reads; a span context manager.
3. The edge binds the trace and the request's span and answers with a traceparent; the job takes the trace and the request's span as its parent.
4. Model requests, agent steps and tool calls are spans.
5. Read by trace on both logs, the finder, the route and the command line; the adapter's stamp for rows that have a request id.

(3) Decisions
- A request that offers only a trace is known by its first 16 characters. Because: Logs, the Admin lookup and X-Request-ID already speak in request ids: the trace names it when nothing else does.
- A request id that came without a trace gets a trace derived from it (its SHA-256), so one request id is always one trace. Because: A collector joins by trace; the main product's rows carry only a request id and must land in the same trace its edge would have made.
- The trace id is a column of its own on PostgreSQL, not a path into the document. Because: Reading one request's events by trace is the point of the id; the index follows the other id columns.
- An agent step and a tool call get a span when they are recorded, not while they run. Because: The agent writes its trace row after the step; the span id is what a collector joins by.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Work in a thread the request did not start carries no trace (a context variable does not cross a bare thread).
- The model-request usage table keeps no trace id; its event does.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Phase 1's fourth gap: every error in the record with a fingerprint (the exception's type and the top frame inside our code), the request, the job or run it belongs to; a rate-limit refusal as an event; the Sessions page and the command line grouping the last days by fingerprint; adoptable by the main product.

(2) Plan
1. Put the fingerprint in dclab_core: type and the innermost frame of our own code, twelve hex characters, a host adds its own package prefixes.
2. Add the fields to the two error kinds and move the contract to v5.
3. Write it where each failure is caught, under the ids already bound there (the job's visit and request through _acting).
4. Group in the finder; expose on the route, the CLI and the Admin page.
5. Test the fingerprint, the grouping, a failed stage through the runner's own branch and a failed job through the worker.

(3) Decisions
- The fingerprint is the exception's type and the innermost frame inside our own packages, never the message. Because: A message quotes values and paths; two projects failing the same way must be one group, and nothing of a table may enter a meta field.
- An error raised outside our code groups by its type alone. Because: A library's frame changes with its version; the type is what the owner can act on.
- The job runner writes error.raised inside _acting, before job.stopped. Because: That is where the job's visit, request and id are bound; the done-when asks for the request id beside the group.
- A limit refusal is an error.raised with status 429 and the limit's kind as where, written explicitly to the workspace's log. Because: It is answered before the visit is bound; the Sessions page should still show a person hitting a limit.
- The contract moves to v5 for two meta fields. Because: The rule from 23.2's review: a kind's fields are part of the contract's shape; older versions read as the current one.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The main product computes its fingerprints with its own package prefixes (own=); until it does, its error rows group by type alone.
- The browser page's errors (ui.error_shown) carry a code, not a fingerprint: the server's error is the one grouped.

- A promotion is the final stage approved; there is no rejection in this product. Because: The product has no model registry; the main product's model_versions is the place for both.

- Every decision of a project shares the project's outcome: a set that learns from it must group by project, as the splits do.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Phase 1's feedback gap: a thumb existed on Home's replies, but nothing kept a score, a correction, a person's own version of a reply, an override, or which version of the agent wrote what was judged. A thumb should create the event with the message's version; an edited reply should become a conversation row whose label is the edit; adoptable by the main product.

(2) Plan
1. The rules in dclab_core: five kinds, seven targets, one check and one verdict function (an edit beats a rejection beats an approval).
2. Stamp what wrote a message: the release (library version and a digest of the prompts, tool schemas and validator) on every chat.agent event, with the message's id.
3. The route resolves the version of the message judged from the log, else the release now.
4. The conversations builder reads the verdicts; rows carry the label and the originals.
5. The buttons (Home's edit, stage explanations' thumbs) and the adapter.

(3) Decisions
- The version is the release (core version and prompts digest) stamped on the chat.agent event, and a thumb inherits the version of the message it judges. Because: A thumb is about the prompts and rules that wrote the message, not the ones running when the person clicked.
- An edit beats a rejection beats an approval; the newest thumb of a message stands. Because: A person who turned a reply down and then wrote the better one gave the label; a changed mind is the last thumb.
- A thumb down ends the example before that reply; it does not drop the whole conversation. Because: What came before was accepted; what the person rejected is not taught, and nothing after it follows from it.
- The original reply stays in edits, never in messages. Because: A set that trains on the edit must not also hold the text the person replaced.
- The experience event moves to v7 for the new fields. Because: The rule since 23.2: a kind's fields are part of the contract's shape.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The release is the whole prompt set's digest: any prompt change makes every earlier message a different version, which is the point, but a finer version per purpose would let an edit be traced to one prompt.
- The intern's own chat page has no buttons yet; its messages carry the version already.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Phase 1's sensitivity gap: nothing told which columns hold a person's data, so example values, category names and top values of an e-mail or a phone column reached the profile, the Home analysis and the intern's description. Classes pii, sensitive and restricted from name tokens and value shapes, never keeping a value; a personal column reaches a model by name only and a dataset never holds its values; adoptable by the main product.

(2) Plan
1. The rules in dclab_core: restricted (secrets, card numbers by Luhn, national ids, IBANs), pii, sensitive, none; a count, flag or rate about such data is not that data.
2. Put the class on the column card and strip what carries values at the source, so every caller is protected.
3. The same at the profile and the Home analysis, which are what the models and the UI read.
4. Carry the class in the event and show it on Home.
5. Prove it with tests that plant personal values in every table the callers read and look for them in every prompt.

(3) Decisions
- Strip at the source (the card, the profile, the analysis) rather than at each model call. Because: A fix at each caller would miss the next one; the data-limit tests then check the callers.
- pii and restricted lose their whole distribution; sensitive keeps it but no category name or example. Because: A phone number's quantiles are a number someone could be called on; a diagnosis' shares are a statistic.
- A count, flag or rate about a kind of data is not that data (email_opens, has_phone, phone_type). Because: Marking them would blind the tools to ordinary features for no protection.
- A bare 'name' column, and name with a person word (customer, patient, member), is pii; product_name is not. Because: The entity's own name is the common case; qualified names of things are not people.
- The event carries the map of column to class, as meta. Because: Names are already in the event; the class lets a later reader know why a column has no values.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Names and shapes are heuristics: a column of free text holding addresses is not caught by either.
- The main product's dataset_columns.sensitivity_class is not in the field lists read; the mapping is described, not coded (23.12).

(5) How you will know it is done
- the rules over the owner's sample data: no ordinary column of the project and public datasets is marked personal

(1) What the package is for
Phase 1's findability gap: what the studio records, where, in what shape, for how long and under which consent lived in prose that could drift; and the questions support and the owner ask most had no home. A generated catalog the gate keeps fresh, the standard questions as functions, a request id as a timeline; adoptable by the main product.

(2) Plan
1. The contract-derived parts (kinds with field classes, points, contracts) in dclab_core, so another host renders the same page.
2. The studio adds what only it knows: where each kind is emitted (by scanning the code), tables with files, retention, consent; a missing description fails the generator.

- The catalog is generated, never edited; descriptions live next to what they describe or in NOTES, and a table or builder with none fails the generator. Because: A page written by hand drifts; the gate that fails when something is added undescribed is what keeps it true.
- Where a kind is emitted is found by scanning the source for its quoted name. Because: No second list to keep; a kind nobody emits shows as emitted by the host.
- The questions are pure functions over lists in dclab_core, with the studio's reader beside them. Because: The main product asks the same questions of its adapted rows; the window is passed in, so nothing reads the clock.
- The request id is a filter of the log itself, not a text search. Because: It is indexed on PostgreSQL and a file store can skip nothing but the lines; text search would match the id inside other fields.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The Admin page has the request field but no menu of the nine questions; the route and the command line have them.
- Owners are found by quoted names: a kind built from variables would show as emitted by the host.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Phase 2 of the owner's plan: an agentic system that understands a problem, breaks a complex one into parts and sub-problems with a big-picture workflow, and composes their solutions; and the rule that every package is adoptable by the main product.

(2) Plan
1. A contract that a person, a rule and later a model can all fill, and one validator that judges all of them the same way.
2. Templates only where the words say the shape; anything else stays one problem, so no single problem is split by accident.
3. A map the main product can hold: one ProblemSpec proposal per sub-problem, the places in the map in a free-form key, the composition once.

(3) Decisions
- The constructor checks shape; validate returns every issue in words. Because: A person's edit can be shown all its reasons at once, and a model's map is judged by the same function as the rules' map.
- A missing unit or moment is a question for the reviewer (24.2), not an unsound map. Because: The words often do not say; refusing the map would force a guess, and a guessed moment is where leakage starts.
- Ranks order the moments: an outcome must be known strictly before a reader's rank, and after its own prediction. Because: One integer per sub-problem is enough to name the leak a late verdict would cause, and to say which read is allowed.
- A composition is built in order from sub-problems and earlier outputs, with the key where two units meet, and leaves out no sub-problem nobody reads. Because: The composer of 24.5 must be able to run it step by step; a result that is left out is a part of the problem silently dropped.
- The fingerprint is the structure (units, moments, families, labels, ranks, needs, reads with keys, steps in order, budget), not the wording. Because: Ledger points and the adapter key on it; two maps that validate differently must not share one.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The templates cover a fraud problem and a two-step routing; the model decomposer (24.2) reads the rest, and is switched on only after a sealed measurement against these rules.
- Whether the main product's parse_objective keeps the free-form key was not readable at the pinned commit.

(5) How you will know it is done
- dev journeys split by the rules: At most 0 of the 15 single-problem sentences of the dev journeys are split into parts (written before the templates).

The request: Phase 2 of the owner's plan: a problem of several parts is solved leaf by leaf, the leaves are composed, and the composed system is scored once on the holdout against the best single leaf.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Phase 2 of the owner's plan: a problem of several parts is solved leaf by leaf, the leaves are composed, and the composed system is scored once on the holdout against the best single leaf.

(2) Plan
1. Each leaf fits on the earlier rows, chooses on the validation rows and hands its scores for validation and holdout to the composition; none scores the holdout.
2. The composition is chosen on validation among every leaf alone and the ways to combine them, a tie to the simpler; the bar is the best leaf on validation, never on the holdout.
3. The holdout opens only when every leaf that was to run has run and the composition is chosen on enough confirmed cases; it is read once, and every later read is a person's written decision.
4. A leaf that cannot run is a blocker with its reason until a person drops it, and a drop is refused once the holdout was read.
5. The record holds names, counts and scores, never a row; the code export reproduces the number from dclab_core alone.

(3) Decisions
- The leaves are the core's own runners on one shared split, not one engine project each. Because: The engine's five stages run their own splits and would read the holdout once per project; one split and one read for the whole is the point of the package. A project per leaf stays open.
- The best leaf the composition must beat is chosen on validation, and taken among every built leaf. Because: A bar chosen on the holdout would move to whichever leaf happens to win there, and a stronger leaf outside the fusion would otherwise never be the bar.
- Rank maximum is a candidate, not a rule: the composition is whatever wins on validation, the best leaf alone included. Because: Rare frauds are visible to one leaf each, so the top of any leaf is what counts; a combination that does not help is not chosen and the result says so.
- The holdout count is carried by the split design, not by the solution map. Because: New routes or a new table change the map but not the rows of the holdout; seeing them again under new routes is a second look.
- The replica's scale was calibrated for statistical power on other seeds (10 to 15) before the acceptance seeds (0 to 2) were run. Because: With few fraudulent bikers a bootstrap over bikers is too wide to tell a gain from chance; scale is chosen for power, never for a result.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The leaves are the core's runners, not one engine project each; a leaf with its own engine run is open.
- No page for the programme and no agent tool for it yet.
- The bootstrap clusters by one entity key; rings also move through accounts.
- The classifier trains on the screen's in-sample scores and is judged on out-of-sample ones: a cross-fitted screen would remove the skew.

(5) How you will know it is done
- replica calibration: Chosen before the acceptance seeds: the fusion beats the best leaf with the interval above zero on every one of the dev seeds 10 to 15 at the final scale.
- programme on the fraud replica, seeds 0 to 2: The composed holdout number beats the best leaf chosen on validation with the paired interval above zero, the holdout read once, on each of three seeds the calibration never saw.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Phase 6 (the owner): finish the understanding team; what was left of 28.4 after the critic: the problem analyst and the data investigator as parallel nodes, the measurement against the single Home agent, and the critic's questions and answers and the briefs captured for training.

(2) Plan
1. Write the tests first: the two readers in one superstep joined as one hand-off, the analyst reading every answer, the walk without the parallel analysis, the critic's question marked in the conversation events.
2. Fan the walk's analysis out to the problem analyst and the data investigator with one Send each, joined by a node that records one step, one hand-off and the pair's cost.
3. Let the analyst read the person's answers given after the analysis before the critic reads the card.
4. Mark the critic's questions in the experience contract and in the conversation examples; give the analyst's hand-offs their training family.
5. Measure the walk on the dev journeys against the single agent's loop, field by field.

(3) Decisions
- The data investigator in the team is the coordinator's own analysis, called unchanged; the problem analyst is a new reading of the first sentence and every answer. Because: The owner's rule for the team is enhance, never replace: every node names an existing function, and only the team behaviour is new.
- The analyst reads again before the critic whenever the person said more since its last reading, not only at the analysis. Because: The answers that matter most to the analyst (the review capacity with its action) are often given after the analysis; read only then, it never saw them.
- The analyst takes only the action from the answers, never the outcome. Because: By the analysis the outcome is settled by the person or by the data; a free reading of the answers bound words that merely name a column as the outcome.
- The analyst's hand-offs are understanding examples, not solution designs. Because: They change the brief, not the design; the brief reaches design examples as the input of the workflow's hand-offs, and calling a reading a design would mislabel the training data.
- The critic's question is marked by a new field on the agent's chat event, which moves the experience contract to v11. Because: The vocabulary is closed: a new field moves the version, and older events are read as the new one.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- A future call inside either reader that takes the draft's turn would deadlock: the walk holds it and the readers run in other threads.
- The analyst's reading of the answers is shown on invented people only; real conversations may state actions the rules' pattern does not read.

(5) How you will know it is done
- the dev journeys through the walk's graph with the team's readers, beside the single Home agent's loop (JRN-022 against JRN-020): the team's brief at least as right as the single agent's on every card field and every part, nothing asked twice (the package's own condition, fixed before the run)

(1) What the package is for
Phase 7 (the owner): a student behind every choice; 29.3 labels the outcome points by what was measured after the choice, from self-play alone and from every workspace.

(2) Plan
1. Write a measured label on each outcome point from the numbers recorded after the choice, where the capture already writes the decision.
2. Record self-play's verified solves again so their ledgers carry the labels, and build the per-point sets from those ledgers into the lake.
3. Test a planted bad choice labelled wrong and read into its set, and self-play rows grouped by solve.

(3) Decisions
- A recipe or family choice is labelled only when one option leads every other by more than their combined fold spread. Because: The highest validation mean inside the folds' noise is no truth: a label copying it marked the rule wrong where it had declined a gap a sixth of a fold standard deviation wide, and a student trained on it would copy noise.
- The metric's direction comes from the engine (a kind's machine, the tabular spec, or the stage record), and nothing is labelled when it is unknown. Because: MAE, MASE and the Brier score are better when lower; ranking by the highest mean labelled the worst regression family as best.
- A tuning is judged on a fresh draw of its replica (the default and the candidate fitted and scored there, a paired bootstrap), and only on self-play. Because: The rule keeps a tuning on validation; any label from the same validation agrees with it or says nothing; the holdout scores only the kept configuration, and scoring the default there too would be a second use of it: the owner's call.
- No label for a holdout read again. Because: A constant written as measured measures nothing, outranks a person's label and contradicts the validator, which allows a person's reuse with a reason.
- The label rule lives in dclab_core (measured.clear_best), its evidence kinds in DecisionLabel v4. Because: The main product's model comparisons can label their choices the same way.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Real projects' tunings stay unlabelled until the owner decides about the holdout.
- The gold family and recipe sets shrink to a few rows after the evaluation seeds and duplicates are dropped.

- self-play's outcome points: Done when: the outcome points have sets with both labels from self-play alone

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Package 34.5 of the phase-10 plan: compare DCLab's engine as it is with FLAML (owner-approved pip install) on the 10 UCI sets, Telco and the expansion samples, same splits, metric and time budget; holdout score with interval, minutes and peak memory per dataset; stored as an evidence campaign; the rule deciding 34.8 fixed before the run. Small budgets on the 8 GB Air.

(2) Plan
1. read the plan, the expansion datasets and the studio engine
2. choose how each engine gets the same split
3. install FLAML and read how it splits
4. write the harness, the rule and the freeze
5. test on a tiny grouped table through the real orchestration
6. review before the real run (results are written once)
7. fix the findings
8. run the bake-off when the machine is free (owner's call)

(3) Decisions
- Run the studio engine (all five stages) rather than the expansion runner's campaign Because: the expansion runner loads only its four datasets; the studio engine is the engine the product runs on any table, and its prepare() gives one bundle both engines can share
- Give FLAML the engine's own training folds as a splitter object Because: FLAML reshuffles rows for its string split types; a splitter object is used as given (no shuffle, no rare-class augment), so both search on the same folds
- Take the engine's holdout predictions by wrapping fit_and_predict during the final stage and check them against the record Because: the record keeps no predictions; refitting would be a second holdout read; the check proves the captured predictions are the recorded ones
- Each engine in its own process Because: its wall time and peak memory are its own, and a crash or the OS ending one on 8 GB does not end the campaign
- FLAML gets the raw tabular columns, not the engine's engineered features Because: a bake-off of engines as they are; the text dataset, where FLAML then sees no text, is reported but not judged by the rule
- A fixed 300 s FLAML budget, the engine's time measured Because: the engine has no time knob; the brief asks for about five minutes per engine per dataset; time never enters the rule
- Rule: FLAML ahead (paired 95% interval above 0) on at least a third of the judged datasets and on more than it is behind; at least 10 judged; a FLAML failure counts as behind Because: the owner's proposal made exact: paired on the same rows is stricter than two overlapping intervals, and failures and early stops cannot bend the count

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- FLAML sees the engine's raw columns, not its engineered features: a no-go would not prove FLAML as a family behind the recipe is useless
- one holdout per dataset: wide intervals on small sets (heart disease, 61 rows) make 'ahead' hard to reach
- the fraud sample keeps the latest 20,000 rows: few positives in the holdout

(5) How you will know it is done
- the harness on a tiny grouped table (420 rows, 30 stores), both engines, FLAML 3 s: same holdout rows, labels, folds and columns; FLAML fitted on training rows only and predicting the holdout once; the engine's captured predictions reproduce its record; intervals around both scores
- the full bake-off, 14 datasets (bakeoff_v1), on an 8 GB MacBook Air: 34.8 goes ahead when FLAML is clearly ahead (paired 95% interval above 0) on at least a third of the datasets both engines finished

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Tables and artifacts do not belong in the database. Put uploaded files, cleaned Parquet tables and exports behind one file storage (a local folder now, S3-compatible later), record each file with its key, size, SHA-256 and content type, and check the hash when a stage loads data.

(2) Plan
1. Map how data files are stored and read today (an explore agent): project and draft documents hold bare file names, and in PostgreSQL mode the workspace id is the folder's absolute path, so moving the folder would lose every project.
2. Give a workspace folder a stable identity: a .dclab_workspace marker holding the old key (the path), so existing workspaces keep their id and a moved folder stays the same workspace.
3. Write files.py: keys relative to the workspace folder, LocalFiles and S3Files, records in a stored_file table (migration 0008) or .dclab_files.json.
4. Record project data, draft uploads and cleaned tables, and the intern's exports; make every read of a project's table go through data_path, which checks the recorded SHA-256 (the engine, the Solution routes, the intern's tools).
5. Write tests, including the moved-folder test on PostgreSQL; run the gate and the reviewer; fix; commit.

(3) Decisions
- The workspace marker stores the folder's old path as its key. Because: Existing PostgreSQL workspaces were keyed by that path; keeping it as the marker's content means no migration of ids, while a moved folder carries its identity with it.
- Every read of a project's table checks the recorded hash, and a changed table is a 409, never modelled. Because: A file that changed on disk after it was recorded would otherwise go straight into a model and silently change the results.
- S3 credentials come only from boto3's default chain; records hold no bucket URL or credential. Because: A file record is shown and copied; it must never carry a secret.
- The intern's export returns keys, not absolute paths. Because: An absolute path leaks the machine's layout and means nothing to another instance or a bucket.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- A workspace whose only identity is its folder path loses its projects in the database when the folder moves.
- Deleting the old table before the new one is stored turns any storage error into data loss.
- Two rules that decide the same name (upload sanitising and storage keys) can disagree and make some uploads fail midway.
- A file that changed on disk after it was recorded goes straight into a model unless every read checks the hash.
- A file record or an error message could carry an S3 credential, a bucket URL or database connection details.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Start the AI and agent layer with one model gateway. At first the owner asked to skip the intern and not depend on it; a few minutes later he changed his mind: build phases A1 and A2 in the plan's order, the intern included, package by package.

(2) Plan
1. Find every place that creates or configures a model client: the Home agent's flow, the intern, the evidence answers, the stage notes (Responses API), the campaign critic CLI and NOOA's research clients.
2. Move the client from intern/llm.py into dclab_rnd/models/client.py and keep intern/llm.py as an alias; make the SDK's own retry count a parameter so the intern's behaviour does not change while the gateway does its own retries.
3. Write the tier and purpose settings, the usage log (a file, or the model_request table on PostgreSQL, migration 0002) and the gateway.
4. Move the Home flow, stage notes, project answers, evidence answers, the critic CLI and the campaign adapter onto the gateway; after the owner's correction, the intern too.
5. Add GET /api/models and the Admin page's model info; add the new settings to .env.example.
6. Run make check-all and an adversarial review in a fresh context; fix every finding with a test; commit.

(3) Decisions
- Purposes, not callers, pick a tier and a timeout, and each purpose says in words what it may be shown. Because: A tier is a cost and privacy choice that belongs to the kind of request; writing what each purpose may see is the basis for A1.3's data-limit test.
- Retry only transient failures, and a stream only before its first word reached the user. Because: Retrying a refusal wastes money; retrying a stream after text was shown would duplicate or contradict what the person already read.
- NOOA's research clients are not swapped but report each request to the usage log. Because: NOOA builds its own clients through litellm; wrapping them keeps the campaign working while every request is still counted.
- Store no key and no prompt in a usage row unless DCLAB_LOG_PROMPTS=1. Because: The usage log is read on Admin pages and in exports; prompts can carry the user's words.
- A failed usage write never loses an answer. Because: The answer was already paid for; logging is secondary to returning it.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Splitting one model setting into tiers can silently change the model a caller uses when an old variable stops applying to it.
- A key must follow its endpoint; a fallback that moves a URL without its key sends one provider's key to another host.
- Any new setting can let tests reach a live model unless the gateway itself refuses live endpoints under test.
- Requests made outside the gateway, by subclassed clients or command-line runs, go uncounted and break the caps built on the usage log.
- Usage rows and API pages can expose credentials or prompts if endpoints and prompts are stored as given.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Add money to the gateway: price each request from one dated table, enforce per-run, per-project and per-workspace caps before a request is sent, and show real spend on the Compute and Admin pages. Never guess a price.

(2) Plan
1. Write dclab_rnd/models/prices.py (or DCLAB_PRICES_FILE) with a date per table; a model without a price is counted in tokens only; a request to a model on this machine is free.
2. Add the cost to the usage log (migration 0003) and the caps to the gateway: the intern session's max_eur (run), the wizard's budget (project, per month), DCLAB_WORKSPACE_MONTHLY_EUR (workspace).
3. Show the euros on Compute and Admin, and how many requests have no price.
4. Update the test that asserted spend is not tracked, since that is exactly what changed.
5. Run check-all and the review; fix the six findings with tests; render the two pages; commit.

(3) Decisions
- Refuse a request when its upper-bound cost could pass a cap, checked and reserved under a lock. Because: Checking 'already over' lets the request that crosses the cap through, and an unlocked check lets concurrent requests near the cap all pass.
- The upper bound is the prompt's characters divided by three times the input price plus max_tokens times the output price. Because: The real token count is known only after the reply; an estimate that is never lower than the truth keeps the cap a cap.
- Never guess a price; an unpriced model is counted in tokens. Because: A guessed price would make a cap look enforced while it is not; showing 'no price' tells the owner what to configure.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- A cap checked as 'already over' lets through the request that crosses it, and concurrent requests near the cap all pass the same check.
- A run's spend kept only in a client object resets whenever the server builds a new client for a message, or restarts.
- Something computed after a paid request, such as its cost, fails and loses both the answer and its usage row.
- Clients that do not send through the gateway, such as the research campaign's, record spend but never ask whether a cap allows the request.
- 'Local' judged loosely makes a remote endpoint free in the log and impossible to cap.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Make the workflow validator impossible to skip: every write tool declares the move it makes, the runtime asks studio.graph.check as the agent before the handler runs, and a refusal is logged and returned to the model with the reason and the rules. The Home agent's draft writes get their own checks.

(2) Plan
1. Read the validator (studio/graph.py) and list which project writes it checks; four (create_project, attach_data, set_settings, propose_solution) were never checked or logged.
2. Write the test first, as a new file while A2.1 was under review: refuse every project write tool and fail when a new write tool has no refusal case.
3. Make registration refuse a write tool without a move, and send every write through its scope's guard: the project guard asks graph.check as the agent; the draft guard checks the pack list and the user's choice, workflow.validate and one preparation at a time.
4. Add graph checks for the four uncovered writes (for example the agent may not replace the data under a solution the owner signed).
5. Run check-all and the review; fix the two findings; commit.

(3) Decisions
- The guard lives in the registry's call path, not in each handler. Because: A handler that checks the graph itself can be written without the check; a registry that refuses to run a write without a guard cannot be bypassed by a new tool.
- A refused Home workflow keeps the current workflow instead of falling back to the template. Because: Falling back silently replaced work the person had already seen with a generic template.
- The create_project transition logs the name but not the user's goal. Because: The goal is the user's free text and the transition log is the future training source (A6.1); the reviewer noted it would carry up to 300 characters of the task.
- create_project's refusal is returned but not logged. Because: Before a project exists there is no log to write to; the exception is written in the status row rather than hidden.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- A write tool registered without a declared move bypasses the validator entirely.
- Moving refusals into the registry changes the shape of the result that callers such as the intern's report loop parse.
- Project writes the old code never checked (create_project, attach_data, set_settings, propose_solution) could let the agent replace data under a signed solution.
- Logging refusals puts the user's free text into the transition log, which later becomes training data.
- The registry's names-level check refusing short calls the Home handlers always defaulted.

(1) What the package is for
Add shadow mode to the gateway: a purpose can name a shadow model that receives the same request; its answer is stored and compared (same tool chosen? same validated output?) but never used. Show agreement rates on the Admin page. Switching a purpose to the tuned model requires a reviewer's approval, recorded in the audit trail, and can be undone in one setting.

(2) Plan
1. Map the gateway: tiers, purposes, Bound, usage, the intern's long-lived client.
2. Write models/routing.py (a purpose's serving tier, its shadow, the history; file or table, migration 0007) and models/shadow.py (compare the first tool call and its arguments, log without prompt, arguments or answer).
3. In the gateway, copy the caller's messages first, answer from the served model, then send the copy to the shadow in a background thread; never return it, never count it in usage or budgets; only a local tier may shadow.

(3) Decisions
- Only a local tier can shadow. Because: A shadow copies every request; locally it costs nothing and no cap needs to see it, and no data goes to another provider.

- Shadow traffic sending data to another provider or adding cost.
- Places that report which model serves falling out of step with the routing.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Here are the GitHub repositories of Hugging Face Chat UI and ML Intern: use them to have that experience in DCLab, locally and one click away.

(2) Plan
1. Check the state of the two repositories: ML Intern is archived and its mode now lives inside Chat UI.
2. Expose the intern's toolbox as a stateless streamable-HTTP MCP server with JSON responses, mounted at /mcp inside the notebook server's lifespan, or standalone on its own port.
3. Exempt /mcp from the browser CSRF token, keeping the host check.
4. Write the launcher: clone Chat UI into a gitignored folder, write its .env.local (model endpoint, MCP_SERVERS pointing at DCLab, ML Intern mode and Hugging Face sign-in only when asked), npm install once, npm run dev.
5. Add the web packages make notebook needs to requirements/base.txt.
6. Verify against the real Chat UI with a mock OpenAI-compatible model, in plain mode and in ML Intern mode, and with the official MCP Python client.
7. Write tests/test_mcp.py and document how to connect on the Intern page and in the README.

(3) Decisions
- DCLab becomes an MCP server that Chat UI attaches to, rather than a fork of Chat UI or ML Intern. Because: ML Intern's repository is archived; a fork would have to be maintained. Over MCP, ML Intern or any tool-capable model can create projects, write contracts, run the five deterministic stages and export notebooks in DCLab, while Hub Jobs and sandboxes stay Hugging Face's.
- The MCP transport is stateless with JSON responses. Because: A plain POST of a JSON-RPC message then works, which keeps the server simple and easy to test.
- /mcp skips the browser CSRF token but keeps the host check. Because: An MCP client is not a browser page and cannot carry the token; the host check still refuses requests from other origins.
- The launcher reads the model key from .env and writes it only into the gitignored Chat UI folder; the key is never typed in a UI or committed. Because: Credentials stay on the machine and out of the repository.
- make clean leaves the Chat UI folder alone. Because: Its install is slow; deleting it on every clean would cost minutes for nothing.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Forking the archived ML Intern and having to maintain it.
- Exempting /mcp from the CSRF token and opening it to requests from other origins.
- The model key leaking into the repository or a UI.
- Dependencies installed in only one environment, so make notebook fails in the one the docs name.
- Verifying only against mocks of both ends.

- Chat UI end to end over MCP: The real Chat UI offers the model DCLab's tools in plain mode and in ML Intern mode, and a DCLab tool call round-trips over /mcp.
- A whole project through the official MCP Python client: No gate: a smoke run showing that a full project can be built through /mcp.

(1) What the package is for
Build the first step of the roadmap that the vision review recommended: turn the five stages into the explicit workflow graph WF-01 to WF-10, where the LLM proposes and deterministic code decides (DCLAB-R20), with allowed moves, prerequisites, gates that only a person can open, and every move logged.

(2) Plan
1. Define the ten steps, the engine stage each one runs (WF-04 to WF-07 one stage each, WF-08 and WF-09 the final stage, WF-01 to WF-03 and WF-10 declared), and the rules attached to each.
2. Derive each step's state from the project (done, current, waiting for a person, running, failed, to do) and a one-character-per-step state string for trajectories.
3. Write check() as a pure function: it reads the project, changes nothing, and returns a verdict with every check, the rules, the evidence and the side effects of the move.
4. Route the engine's execute and approve, the intern's tools and the API through check(); a refused move raises GraphBlocked with the verdict.
5. Append every verdict, allowed or not, with the state before it and its outcome, to transitions.jsonl.
6. Add the gates as per-project policy, off by default; add a Graph tab on the project page and get_graph and check_move for the intern.
7. Write tests/test_graph.py and update the studio test that reran the final stage.

(3) Decisions
- check() is pure; the effect and the log are separate steps. Because: The UI and the intern can ask what a move would do without doing it, and the same function decides for every caller.
- Some invariants hold whatever the policy: no skipped steps, only a person approves a gate, the agent never reuses the holdout or changes an earlier choice after the holdout was used, and a person who reruns the final stage gives a reason that is kept in the evidence. Because: These are the rules that leakage-safe evaluation depends on (holdout once, PIT-006); they must not depend on habit.
- The contract-signature and holdout-approval gates are per-project policy, off by default. Because: Existing flows and tests keep working; a team that wants the gates turns them on.
- A verdict has three outcomes: allowed, blocked, or needs a person. Because: Some refusals can be lifted by a person (a written reason, a signature) and some never by the agent; the caller must know which.
- Every verdict and outcome is logged, refused moves included. Because: The log is the audit trail now and the trajectory data the policy model needs later, and refused moves are the negative examples it must learn.
- A signed contract stores the contract's hash; changing the contract invalidates the signature. Because: A signature must apply to the contract as signed, not to whatever it was edited into later.
- Three revisits are allowed on purpose (a leak reopens the contract, the screen sends you back to the features, a shift needs a new split), and the contract can be reopened from any step. Because: Going back is a normal part of honest work; the graph names it instead of forbidding it.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- A validator that the engine calls but the intern's tools or the API bypass, so one caller can still skip a step or reuse the holdout.
- A check() with side effects, so asking what a move would do already changes the project.
- Gates switched on by default, breaking the flows and tests that run the stages without a signature or an approval.
- A contract signature that stays valid after the contract it signed is edited.
- Logging only allowed moves, which loses the refused ones the policy model must learn from.

The only guard in execute was 'run the previous stage first'.

The intern could read the holdout, change a recipe and read it again until the score pleased it. - Keep counting holdout uses and only warn: set aside because the counter already rose without stopping anything, and a warning the agent can ignore is not a guard.

test_holdout_reuse_needs_a_person_with_a_reason_and_never_the_agent; the studio test now reruns the final stage with a reason and checks it is recorded.

A person can still reuse the holdout by writing a reason. The graph keeps the reason with the stage's evidence but does not judge whether it is a good one.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
The feature recipes took logs and ratios of factorized category codes. Keep the codes out of derived features, then treat them as categories inside training folds, and measure on identical training folds, never the holdout, whether a proper encoding recovers the lift that arithmetic on codes appeared to give.

(2) Plan
1. Read the categorical declarations already kept per dataset in the agentic catalog and resolve code columns from them, with the heuristic as fallback.
2. Keep codes out of every derived feature in FeatureEngineer, the expansion recipes and the notebook; fix them once per project on training rows and record them.
3. Re-check informally on identical training folds that the old behaviour reproduces EXP-008 and EXP-028, and see what removing code arithmetic costs.
4. One-hot encode codes in the notebook's encoder with levels learned on each fit fold (top 40, unseen levels all zero) and route them to the one-hot branch in the exported notebook.
5. Write category_codes_v1: CAT-001 (playbook ladder, 3x3 repeated folds whose first repeat is the campaign's own), CAT-002 (the notebook's recipes and folds).
6. Add CAT-003 and CAT-004 for native LightGBM categorical splits on the same folds, with one sensitivity variant declared before any native result.
7. List the affected old records in evidence/README.md; regenerate the index, SFT and research indexes; run rd-check.

(3) Decisions
- Declarations win over the heuristic. Because: The heuristic misses codes with more levels (native-country, day_of_week) and would misread letter recognition's integer shape statistics as codes.
- FeatureEngineer keeps codes as numbers by default and gains an opt-in one_hot_codes flag, not a new ladder stage. Because: Encoding is orthogonal to the derivation rungs; changing raw would change every model_building_50_v1 rerun (CAT-001 shows the current code reproduces them exactly); and the ladder's LightGBM gains nothing measurable from it.
- Records made before the change export with codes as numbers. Because: The exported notebook must reproduce exactly what the engine evaluated then.
- Keep one-hot in the notebook after the native test. Because: For LightGBM no encoding was distinguishable at this data size, and one-hot is the rule-compliant one that pays for linear models.
- Declare min_data_per_group = 20 as the only native variant, before seeing any native result. Because: LightGBM's default of 100 is large next to 800 to 3,200 training rows; varying more settings after seeing results would be tuning on the comparison.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Fixing the encoding to recover a lift that was never real, because the original lift was measured on only a few folds.
- Resolving code columns by a heuristic that misses codes with many levels or mistakes integer measurements for codes.
- Changing FeatureEngineer's defaults and so breaking the exact reproduction of every recorded campaign result.
- Comparing encodings on folds that differ, so a difference reflects the split rather than the encoding.
- Passing codes straight to LightGBM's native categorical input, where negative values are read as missing.

(5) How you will know it is done
- reproduction of the recorded campaign: On the first repeat's folds the legacy arm must reproduce model_building_50_v1's feature-stage ROC-AUC exactly.
- was the derived-recipe lift real: Legacy derived stage minus raw over 9 folds; real only if the corrected 95% interval excludes zero.
- does one-hot recover the lift: One-hot raw minus the legacy derived stage, corrected 95% interval above zero.

The request: Send the campaign's 50 bounded review tasks to a capable LLM critic and keep only cited, reviewed conclusions as durable memory. Later: make sure a critic's wrong objection never becomes memory or training data.

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
Send the campaign's 50 bounded review tasks to a capable LLM critic and keep only cited, reviewed conclusions as durable memory. Later: make sure a critic's wrong objection never becomes memory or training data.

(2) Plan
1. Give the critic one bounded task per experiment: the evidence bundle, the claims, and a required answer format (evidence, interpretation, decision, risks, smallest next test).
2. Run the 50 reviews and render the report; keep the model's challenges with an id and a severity.
3. When building the knowledge layer, read the critic's challenges against the recorded numbers before using them.
4. Write critic_gate.py: parse each stage's selection rule (tolerance, std penalty, acceptance margin) and recompute the choice from the recorded rows.

- Recompute the rule rather than ask a second model to judge the first. Because: Every stage records its rule beside the numbers it was applied to, so a deterministic recomputation settles the dispute.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- A critic's fluent but wrong objection becoming durable memory or training data.
- Letting the critic rewrite a measured metric or approve deployment.
- Judging the critic with another model that adds its own errors.
- A gate hard-wired to ROC-AUC that misjudges campaigns selecting on other metrics.
- Storing free chat as memory, which nobody can later check against a result file.

(5) How you will know it is done
- critic gate consistency: Every recomputable selection must agree with the choice the result recorded.

(2) Plan
1. Write the manifest first: for each experiment its question, hypothesis, dataset and source.
2. Lock a holdout per dataset before any analysis; cap each table at 4,000 rows for the first pass with 3-fold stratified CV.
3. Stage 1: profile training rows only (missingness, duplicates, positive rate, random-split PSI as a smoke check).
4. Stage 2: declare decision-time exclusions (bank duration, shoppers PageValues), run heuristic proxy checks and a synthetic canary, and measure safe vs unsafe CV.
5. Stage 3: compare the feature ladder (raw, logs, ratios, interactions, full, selected) with folds-fitted features; pick the smallest matrix within 0.002 ROC-AUC of the best.
6. Stage 4: screen five families on identical folds, ranked by mean minus 0.25 x fold std.

- Rank model families by mean minus 0.25 x fold std, then tune only the chosen family. Because: Stability matters as much as the mean; tuning every family multiplies selection on the same folds.

- Looking at scores before writing each experiment's question and hypothesis, which turns 50 runs into a pile rather than a study.
- Reading a dataset's holdout more than once while choosing recipes or models.
- Rewarding every extra column, so feature dilution never shows up as a negative result.
- Tuning every model family on the same folds and multiplying the selection.
- Trusting a silent leakage detector that was never shown to catch a planted canary.

- leakage audit, safe vs unsafe training CV: Declared decision-time exclusions are removed; the apparent lift is unsafe minus safe CV ROC-AUC, measured on training folds only.
- feature ladder selection: Smallest matrix within 0.002 mean CV ROC-AUC of the best stage.
- final holdout, read once per dataset: Model and settings locked on training CV; a tuned candidate accepted only above the declared margin; holdout scored once with a bootstrap 95% interval.

The owner: 'make sure all data must capture and record and store for all 6 models we have', with the plan for more ability (S8) approved; capture correctness first.

(2) Plan
1. Count the real-table records by the lake's split and the store's.
2. Ask the other session (the store's author) before changing the split.

(3) Decisions
- The fix is in dclab_core.datasets.split_of, the one function every set builder and the store's shaper call. Because: One place: the store, the dataset builders and the curriculum read it; a second mapping in the store would drift.

- Twins move only to dev, in lake.split_of itself. Because: Dev is neither trained on nor read as a blind exam: no table becomes train or sealed, so no exam already read changes; and every caller (store, screens, homework, collector) agrees at once.

(1) Root cause
The requests counter is keyed by floor(time / 60). The protect middleware charges the request with its own time.time() before call_next; the route reads the window with a second time.time() after the visit is marked, the active jobs are listed, the month's model spend is read and the budgets file is opened. When a minute ends between the two, the read lands in the next, empty window. The other suspect is ruled out: the trace shows one charge (the quota request; the sign-in requests come before the person is known) and it comes before the read. On an idle machine the two reads were 14 to 723 ms apart (median 247 ms over 20 requests); the parallel suite under memory pressure stretches that.

(2) Why it matters
A red gate on a correct change now and then (a minute boundary inside a gap of a quarter of a second to several seconds), sending someone to look for a limiter bug that is not there; the product's answer was right. A test that fails by chance teaches people to ignore red results, and a real failure then hides among the false ones.

In the test, replace dclab_rnd.limits' reference to the time module with a frozen clock (types.SimpleNamespace with time() returning 1_700_000_010) around the sign-in and the quota request, so the charge and the read use one window; assert exactly one request for the person and the workspace.

- Make the page read the window its own request was counted in (the charge's time carried in a context variable): set aside, because the current minute is the right answer for a fixed window, and it adds product code to fix a test's timing.
- Patch time.time globally: set aside, because it freezes the session cookies, the visit and every other clock in the app, not only the limiter's.
- Retry the read, or accept zero when a minute has just ended: set aside, because the test would no longer prove that the page counts its own request.

(4) The test that proves it
The reproduction (the clock crossing a minute between the charge and the read) fails the old test and passes the new one, whose frozen clock replaces the crossing one; tests.test_limits: 12 tests OK.

(5) What stays open
Two things stay open. First, test_requests_a_minute_and_the_others_are_unaffected still runs on the real clock; it allows one crossing of the minute (429 by the 83rd request against a limit of 40) and would fail only if two crossings fit in a hundred requests, about 1.5 s a request. (2) Plan
1. read the kinds' cases and acceptance runs, the replicas, the engine's records, the campaigns' layout and the contract registry
2. the contracts in dclab_core (challenge_pack: pack, key, observed, grade) with the code vocabulary and the partition rule
3. the groups family generator with its knobs and the reference statements
4. the studio side: packs written apart from their keys, a solve from the public folder, observe a run

- The new contract is challenge_pack, not challenge Because: dclab_core.challenge and dclab_rnd.challenge already name 16.13's challenge mode (briefs)

- the replica converter and the 'every replica grades as today' test are not built (named in the plan's H0)

- the reference arm on 60 variants (30 learning, 30 check): every variant solvable by its key's statements; the honesty guard's threshold set above every honest solve
- the baselines (LRN-001 check, LRN-002 learning; 20 variants each): every scored variant solvable

The owner asked to record everything first, then continue the harness-learning plan with the local model (Qwen3.5-4B now, 9B later), allowing 9 GB of swap. H3 needs a solver that repeats for free, so before any lesson is probed the local model must show it can finish the homework at all.

(2) Plan
1. measure what the local server returns as reasoning with probe_reasoning before choosing it
2. write the solver: a gateway with every tier local, the person's request from the brief only, the attempt as an acceptance Run for the grader
3. write the pilot and its CLI command with the gate fixed before the run
4. test with a scripted intern that states what the key would state, then review, then run the pilot live at no cost

(3) Decisions
- Ollama's /v1 serves the local solver Because: the probe read its reasoning field and its tool calls; mlx_lm.server returns no tool calls for Qwen3.5 (mlx-lm #1293)
- A learning attempt is its own workspace folder with its events and decisions beside its projects Because: the store then finds one whole attempt, and a trainer can read the moves with the project they changed
- An exam attempt records nothing and its model exchanges keep their shape only Because: an exam problem must never become training data, or the check and sealed scores stop measuring anything new
- A homework that broke before the model answered makes the run invalid, not a fail Because: a stopped server or a crash in DCLab's code would otherwise be stored as evidence that the model cannot do the work
- The pilot's result files are named _pilot Because: a baseline reader filters by split; a pilot named _learning would look like a baseline
- A pilot pauses between homeworks and goes on where it stopped Because: the owner stops the laptop when needed; a homework takes about 45 minutes on it

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- a kept attempt's model exchanges go to the workspace's folder, not the attempt's
- the small model may think long and answer nothing; the pilot measures it

(5) How you will know it is done
- the reasoning probe on Ollama with the local Qwen: the reasoning field read

Plan the work.

(1) What the package is for
The owner found two bugs in the path a local Qwen model takes: the OpenAI-compatible client ignores the reply's reasoning field (lost training data) and never sends it back (the agent forgets its plan from turn to turn). They asked for the reasoning kept under either name servers use, sent back per endpoint setting, Qwen's preserve_thinking template setting turned on, and tool arguments sent back as objects.

(2) Plan
1. read the client, the tier settings, the gateway's transport and exchange log, and the test fakes
2. three per-tier options in models.settings.options(), chosen per endpoint and never from the model's name
3. the client reads the reply's reasoning under the field, in complete and stream, and sends it back in assistant_message
4. chat_template_kwargs in extra_body on every request; tool arguments as dicts when the tier says object
5. the gateway passes the options, counts the earlier reasoning in its estimate, keeps the tools offered in the exchange
6. a probe command through the gateway; tests with SDK-level fakes; the adversarial review

(3) Decisions
- The reasoning field is a per-tier setting (none by default), never guessed from the model's name Because: Hermes Agent's tracker shows guessing by name breaks on each new server; a server that returns no field is asked for none
- out['thinking'] = [{'text': reasoning}] beside out['reasoning'] Because: the exchange log and store/sets/llm.py already read that shape from the Anthropic transport; nothing downstream changes
- Tool arguments go back as the OpenAI wire string by default and as dicts only with TOOL_ARGUMENTS=object Because: OpenAI and most servers require the string; Qwen's template renders a string badly; the parsed tool_calls keep dicts in every case
- The exchange keeps tool names and a hash always, the schemas whole only with a whole exchange Because: a model trained on the record must learn what it could call at that moment; schemas are static definitions, never cell values

- The probe is the owner's command, never a test Because: D3: tests never reach a live model; which server passes reasoning through is unverified and must be measured

- a server that rejects extra_body.chat_template_kwargs fails every request of that tier until the setting is removed
- the probe's made-up conversation is kept in the exchange log under project id 'probe'; the sets do not skip it yet (reviewer's note)
- a shadow tier's server that rejects an unknown message key (the served tier's reasoning field) fails the shadow call: logged, never used

- the new tests and the 16 files around models settings, gateway, client and the exchange log: every test passes

The owner found check-all too slow and asked to make the process as fast as possible, using up to 90% of the Mac (8 GB, 8 cores), swap up to 6 GB, yellow memory pressure accepted, only red not.

(2) Plan
1. Measure where the time goes: 125 files, 8 cores, 8 GB; 111 files waited for memory; two passes of the whole suite in sequence.
2. Fork every test file from one process that has imported the heavy libraries once.
3. Start files by macOS's own memory pressure (green and yellow), not by free memory; two workers more than the cores.
4. Run rd-gates, the agent tests and the flows beside the suite; a per-package gate (affected files, PostgreSQL on the files that check it); a gate on a commit in its own worktree.

(3) Decisions

- Memory pressure decides when a file starts: green or yellow, never red. Because: The owner's rule; free memory undercounts what macOS can compress and swap without slowing down.

- The import graph chooses the files, but central modules reach most of them. Because: The session recorder and the contracts' base are imported almost everywhere: most changes reach 110 of 125 files; the saving is in the PostgreSQL pass (30 files that check it) and the flows.
- check-all closes a milestone; check-quick gates a package; check-commit runs a gate on a commit in its own worktree. Because: Work goes on while the gate runs; a push waits for it.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Forking after preloading assumes the libraries start no threads at import (one-thread settings are set first).
- Two gates at once would share the per-worker test databases: one gate at a time.

(5) How you will know it is done
- whole suite on files: faster than 479 s with every test passing
- check-all: faster than about 19 minutes, passing
